mainTopic: Separate oaths from naming several items, and how an oath can take effect on food the תורה already forbids
overview: The גמרא finishes explaining why the משנה repeats 'פת' before each grain: the extra word shows he meant a separate oath for each kind of bread. It then asks why naming wine, oil, and honey makes him liable for each, since nothing there is extra. רב פפא says the drinks were in front of him, and the גמרא works through several shorter wordings until it reaches 'these and their types.' רב אחא בריה דרב איקא instead says a friend had pressed him to drink these drinks, so naming them was extra. The גמרא then quotes a משנה about a false שבועת הפקדון, together with רבי יוחנן's rule that the grains combine to a פרוטה and a dispute about whether a list also holds a general oath. רבא explains that this dispute cannot apply to our oath, because a person who is מושבע ועומד cannot take on a second oath. Finally, the גמרא resolves why inedible food makes him exempt while נבילות make him liable, and asks how an oath can take hold on food already forbidden from הר סיני. רב, שמואל and רבי יוחנן answer that he included permitted foods too, and ריש לקיש answers that it only works with a half-measure. The amud ends as ריש לקיש begins to explain why he does not accept the idea of איסור כולל here; his answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why he could not just list the grains without saying bread each time
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the idea that he could have said one short oath covering all three grains. A shorter wording might have meant only bread made from a mix of all three.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe [if he had said it that shorter way, it would have meant only bread made] from a mixture [of the grains]?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion that the oath-taker could simply have listed the grains together. It points out that such wording could be misunderstood as referring only to mixed-grain bread.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier suggestion was that naming each grain only served to keep the oath from covering other foods, so a short list would have been enough. The גמרא answers that a short list is not enough: it could sound like one kind of bread made from all three grains together. So naming each grain separately has a real purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: But perhaps (introduces a possibility that weakens an argument)
By way of a mixture, meaning bread made from mixed grains

phrases.english: But perhaps [it would mean bread made] from a mixture?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion from the previous part of the daf about the wording 'פת חטים ופת שעורים ופת כוסמין'.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that a shorter, combined list of grains would have been enough.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A combined list could be read as covering only mixed-grain bread, so it would not clearly forbid each kind of bread.

steps.title: Repeating the word bread shows each grain is a separate oath
steps.stepSummary: Even to avoid the mixture problem, he could have said 'and so of barley, and so of spelt.' Repeating the word 'bread' each time must teach that each one is its own oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say: '[Bread of wheat] and so of barley and so of spelt.' Why do I need 'bread,' 'bread' again? Learn from this: it is to separate them [into separate oaths].
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the mixture problem could have been avoided with the wording 'and so of barley, and so of spelt.' It concludes that repeating 'פת' each time must be there to make separate oaths.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'וכן של' already makes clear that each grain is a separate kind of bread, not a mixture, without repeating the word 'bread.' So repeating 'פת' is extra wording. The extra word teaches לחלק: each grain counts as a separate oath, so he brings a separate קרבן for each one.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him say (the גמרא proposes a better wording)
Why do I need it? (points to extra wording)
To separate, here meaning to make separate liabilities

steps.whatToRemember: In the bread case, repeating the word 'פת' before each grain is extra wording, and it shows he meant separate oaths, so he is liable separately for each.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the question in the next steps: in the drinks case there is no repeated word, so where does the separate liability come from?

phrases.english: Let him say: 'And so of barley'
'And so of spelt';
Why do I need 'bread,' 'bread'?
Learn from it: to separate [them].
phrases.notes: Separate oaths, so he is liable for each kind of bread on its own.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts that the mixture worry is real, but shows it could be solved without repeating 'bread', so the repetition must teach separate oaths.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The repeated word 'פת' is extra and comes to make each grain a separate oath (לחלק).

steps.title: Quoting the משנה about an oath not to drink
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: one who swore 'I will not drink' and drank many drinks is liable only once. The quote is cut short, and the case of naming specific drinks follows in the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'An oath that I will not drink,' and he drank many liquids: he is liable only once, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line of the משנה about drinks. It is setting up a question about the rest of that משנה, where naming wine, oil, and honey makes him liable for each.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A general oath 'I will not drink' is one oath, so drinking many liquids brings only one קרבן. The 'etc.' points to the rest of the משנה: if he named wine, oil, and honey, he is liable for each one. That second part is what the גמרא will question.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath that I will not drink
He is liable for only one (קרבן)

phrases.english: 'An oath that I will not drink'
and he drank many liquids,
he is liable only once, etc.
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' points to the rest of the משנה: naming wine, oil and honey makes him liable for each one.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אֶשְׁתֶּה וְשָׁתָה מַשְׁקִין הַרְבֵּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the bread case to the parallel drinks case in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general oath not to drink is one oath; drinking many liquids brings only one liability. (The משנה goes on to say that naming several drinks brings a separate liability for each.)

steps.title: In the drinks case there is no extra word, so why separate liabilities?
steps.stepSummary: The bread case worked because 'פת' was repeated. In the drinks case nothing is repeated, so naming the drinks may only have been meant to leave other drinks permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is fine there [with the bread], since you said the repeated 'bread, bread' is extra and comes to create liability. But here, what is there to say? Perhaps he comes to free himself from other liquids!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה's ruling that one who named wine, oil, and honey is liable for each one. Unlike the bread case, there is no extra word to teach separate oaths.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the bread case, the extra 'פת' proved separate oaths. In the drinks case, naming the drinks may have a simple purpose: to keep the oath from covering other drinks such as water. If that is the reason for the wording, there is no proof he meant separate oaths, so he should be liable only once.

keyTerms.meaning: It is fine / understandable (sets up a contrast)

phrases.english: It is fine there, since you said
the 'bread,' 'bread' is extra for him, [and comes] for liability;
but here, what was there to say?
Perhaps to exempt himself
from other liquids he comes!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the conclusion of step 2 to show that the drinks case in step 3 lacks the same proof.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that naming wine, oil, and honey makes him liable for each one separately.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Separate liability came from extra wording in the bread case. The drinks case has no extra wording, and naming the drinks can be explained as limiting the oath so other drinks stay permitted.

steps.title: רב פפא: the drinks were sitting in front of him
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the drinks were in front of him. To limit the oath he could have just said 'these', so naming each drink shows he meant separate oaths.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Here we are dealing with a case where [the drinks] are placed before him, since he could have said, 'An oath that I will not drink these.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge by placing the משנה's case where the wine, oil, and honey were in front of the oath-taker.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the drinks were in front of him, the short way to limit the oath was to point and say 'these' (אלו). Since he named each drink instead, the naming is extra. Just like the extra 'פת', it shows he meant separate oaths.

keyTerms.meaning: Here we are dealing with (narrowing the case)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Here we are dealing with [drinks] placed before him,
for he could have said
'An oath that I will not drink these.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: הָכָא בְּמוּנָּחִין לְפָנָיו עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 4 by narrowing the case in the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) so that the naming of the drinks becomes extra wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Naming each drink might only have been meant to keep other drinks permitted, so he should be liable once.
steps.terutzMaskana: When the drinks are in front of him, 'these' would have been enough; naming each one is extra and makes separate oaths.

steps.title: Saying 'these' might have forbidden only these specific drinks
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב פפא: the word 'these' is not the same as naming the drinks. It could forbid only those exact cups and allow other wine, oil, and honey.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps [had he said 'these', it would mean] it is these that I will not drink, but others I will drink?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא's claim that the oath-taker could simply have said 'these.' That wording would have meant something different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'אלו' points to the specific liquids in front of him, so other wine, oil, or honey would still be allowed. Naming 'wine, oil, honey' forbids those kinds of drinks in general. So naming the drinks is not extra after all, and the proof of separate oaths falls apart again.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not saying the oath limits other drinks like water. It is saying 'these' would forbid only these exact portions, while naming the kinds forbids all wine, oil, and honey.

phrases.english: But perhaps it is these that I will not drink,
[but] others I will drink?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב פפא's answer in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's claim that the oath-taker could have said 'these' instead of naming the drinks.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'These' and naming the kinds of drinks do not mean the same thing. 'These' forbids only the portions in front of him, while naming the kinds forbids all such drinks, so naming them has its own purpose and is not extra.

steps.title: He could have said 'drinks like these'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a better wording for limiting the oath: 'I will not drink drinks like these.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if he only wanted to limit his oath, he could have said: 'An oath that I will not drink drinks like these.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the last challenge by offering a different short phrase the swearer could have used. That phrase would have limited his oath to these kinds of drinks without naming each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 showed that 'these' alone is too narrow, because it covers only the cups in front of him. So the גמרא tries 'like these', which seems to stretch to the same kinds of drinks. If that wording was available and he still named each drink, the naming must mean separate oaths.

phrases.english: Rather, [he could have] said:
"An oath that I will not drink [drinks] like these."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 6's objection by offering a broader wording than 'these'.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'These' only covers the exact cups, so it is not the same as naming the drinks.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Like these' would have covered the kinds of drinks, so naming them must mean something more.

steps.title: 'Like these' could mean the amount
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects 'like these', because it might refer to the size of the drink and not to its kind.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps he means: amounts like these I will not drink, but less than this or more than this I will drink?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the wording it just suggested. 'Like these' is unclear and could be about how much he drinks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'like these' could mean 'this exact amount', it does not cleanly limit the oath to these kinds of drinks. So it is not a true replacement for naming the drinks. The proof that naming means separate oaths falls apart again.

phrases.english: Perhaps [it means] like these [amounts] I will not drink;
but less than this and more than this I will drink?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording offered in step 7.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Like these' could refer to amount, so it does not mean the same thing as naming the kinds of drinks.

steps.title: He could have said 'from these types'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries another wording: 'I will not drink from the type of these.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, for example, he could have said: 'An oath that I will not drink from the type of these.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a third wording that talks clearly about kinds of drinks, not amounts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'type' removes the worry about amount from step 8. If this wording was available and he named each drink anyway, the naming should mean separate oaths.

phrases.english: Rather, for example, [he could have] said:
"An oath that I will not drink from the type of these."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8 by switching from 'like these' to 'type of these'.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Type of these' clearly refers to kinds of drinks.

steps.title: 'These types' might leave the cups themselves allowed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects 'from the type of these', because it could forbid other drinks of that kind while leaving the drinks in front of him allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps he means: the type of these I will not drink, but these very drinks themselves I will drink?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the new wording. 'Type of these' might point only to other drinks of the same kind and not to the actual cups in front of him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the opposite problem from step 6. 'These' covered only the cups, and 'type of these' might cover only the other drinks of that kind. Neither wording alone matches naming the drinks.

keyTerms.meaning: These themselves, the very same ones

phrases.aramaic: וְדִלְמָא מִין אֵלּוּ הוּא דְּלָא שָׁתֵינָא,
phrases.english: But perhaps it is the type of these that I will not drink,
but these themselves I will drink?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדִלְמָא מִין אֵלּוּ הוּא דְּלָא שָׁתֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording offered in step 9.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Type of these' might cover only other drinks of that kind and leave the actual drinks in front of him allowed.

steps.title: He could have said 'these and their types'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא settles on a wording that covers both: 'I will not drink these and their types.' Since he named each drink instead, he meant separate oaths.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say: 'that I will not drink these and their types.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא puts the two earlier wordings together into one phrase that covers everything. This ends רב פפא's line of reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'These' covers the cups in front of him, and 'their types' covers other drinks of the same kind. That short phrase would have done everything naming the drinks does. So naming wine, oil and honey one by one must make each one its own oath.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב פפא's line, the swearer could have said 'these and their types'. Since he named each drink instead, he meant a separate oath for each one.

phrases.english: Let him say: "that I will not drink these and their types."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 10 by joining 'these' and 'their types' into one phrase.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Joins the two earlier wordings so all the gaps are covered
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every short wording left some gap, so naming the drinks might just be a way to limit the oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'These and their types' would fully limit the oath, so naming each drink shows separate oaths.

steps.title: רב אחא: a friend kept pressing him to drink
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא explains the משנה differently. His friend pressed him to drink wine, oil and honey. Saying 'I won't drink with you' would have been enough, so naming each drink makes him liable for each one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא son of רב איקא said: We are dealing with a case where his friend was pressing him, saying, 'Come drink wine, oil and honey with me.' He could have just said, 'An oath that I will not drink with you.' Why did he need to say 'wine, oil and honey'? To be liable for each one separately.
steps.whatsHappening: A new אמורא offers a different way to explain the משנה. He sets it in a real situation where naming the drinks was clearly not needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אחא does not need to search for a better wording the way רב פפא did. The friend had already named the drinks, so a simple refusal would have covered them. Repeating each drink by name must therefore mean a separate oath for each.

keyTerms.meaning: Pressing someone, urging him over and over

steps.whatToRemember: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא: the friend named the drinks, so a simple 'I won't drink with you' would have been enough. Naming each drink means a separate liability for each.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explanation does not depend on finding a better wording the swearer could have used, which is what רב פפא's line had to work through step by step before reaching 'these and their types'.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rav Aḥa son of Rav Ika said:
We are dealing with [a case] where his friend was pressing him [to drink],
who said to him:
"Come drink wine, oil and honey with me."
For he could have said:
"An oath that I will not drink with you,"
so why do I need "wine, oil and honey"?
To make him liable for each and every one.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a new answer to step 4's question, apart from רב פפא's line.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Sets the משנה in a specific situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Naming the drinks might only have been meant to leave other drinks allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since the friend's invitation already named the drinks, repeating them by name means a separate oath for each.

steps.title: A related משנה about a false oath on a deposit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה about a שבועת הפקדון. A general denial is one oath. Naming each grain makes him liable for each one.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in a משנה elsewhere: someone says, 'Give me the wheat, barley and spelt of mine that you are holding.' If the holder swears, 'I swear you have nothing with me,' he is liable for only one. If he swears, 'I swear I don't have your wheat, barley and spelt,' he is liable for each and every one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings in a different משנה that is similar to our case. It is setting up a discussion that will be compared to our oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same idea as our משנה, but in the setting of a deposit oath. A general word like 'nothing' makes one oath. Listing each grain by name makes a separate oath for each grain.

keyTerms.meaning: Liable, here meaning he must bring a קרבן

phrases.english: We learned there: 'Give me wheat and barley
phrases.notes: This משנה is about a שומר who falsely denies holding someone's deposit.

phrases.english: and spelt that I have in your hand,'
'I swear that you have nothing in my hand':
he is liable for only one.
'I swear that you do not have in my hand
wheat and barley and spelt':
he is liable for each and every one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic by quoting a משנה from elsewhere about general versus named items. Its dispute (step 15) is later tested against our oath in steps 16–17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general denial counts as one oath. Naming each grain makes him liable for each grain separately.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the grains combine to reach a פרוטה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that even if all the grains together are worth only one פרוטה, they combine and make him liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: even a פרוטה from all of them combines.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן adds a rule to that משנה. The different grains can add up together to reach the minimum value of a פרוטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A deposit oath needs at least a פרוטה's worth to make him liable. רבי יוחנן says the three grains can be counted together to reach that amount. He does not say which part of the משנה he means, and that question opens the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The smallest coin, the minimum value for liability

phrases.english: And רבי יוחנן said:
Even a peruta from all of them combines.
phrases.notes: All three grains together can add up to a פרוטה's worth, even if no single grain does.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a rule about minimum value to the משנה just quoted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The grains combine to reach the פרוטה minimum for liability.

steps.title: רב אחא and רבינא argue: is there also a general oath?
steps.stepSummary: One says he is liable only for the specific named items. The other says he is also liable for a general oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא and רבינא disagree about this. One says: he is liable for the specific items but not for the general one. The other says: he is also liable for the general one.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים argue about the second case, where he named each grain. Does that oath also include a general oath of 'nothing,' on top of the named ones?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first view, naming the grains makes only specific oaths, so רבי יוחנן's combining rule must be about the first case, the general 'nothing' oath. In the second view, the named oath also holds a general oath, so even in the second case the grains can combine to a פרוטה for that general oath.

keyTerms.meaning: The specific items, each named one
The general statement that covers everything

steps.confusionAlert: The argument is not about whether he is liable for each grain. Both agree he is. The argument is only about whether there is an extra general oath on top.

phrases.english: Rav Acha and Ravina disagree about it;
one said: for the specifics he is liable,
for the general he is not liable;
phrases.notes: 'The general' means a hidden overall oath of 'I have nothing of yours,' inside the named list.

phrases.english: and one said: for the general he is also liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Argues about how the named-items case works, which decides where רבי יוחנן's rule applies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One view: a named list makes only specific oaths. Other view: it makes a general oath as well.

steps.title: How does this apply to our case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the rule is in our משנה's oath, in light of this dispute.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the dispute back to our own משנה and asks how it works there. This question sets up the next discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our oath also names separate items. The גמרא wants to know if the same argument about an extra general oath applies here as well.

phrases.english: Here, what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the רב אחא and רבינא dispute back to our משנה's oath.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the dispute about an extra general oath also applies to the oath in our משנה.

steps.title: רבא: The deposit case cannot be compared to our oath
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects the comparison to שבועת הפקדון. There, every oath carries its own liability. Here, a general oath would already bind him, so specific oaths could not take effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: How can you compare these? In the deposit case, a person can be liable for both the general oath and the specific oaths, because if he swears falsely and then swears again, he is liable twice. Here, if you think the general oath counts, why would he be liable for the specific items? He is already under oath!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question from Step 16. He says the argument about deposit oaths does not carry over to our משנה, because the two kinds of oath work differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A false oath about a deposit is a sin each time it is said, so a general oath and specific oaths can both make him liable. An oath not to eat creates a prohibition, and a second oath cannot take effect on something already forbidden by an oath. So in our משנה, if the general oath counted, the specific oaths would have nothing left to add.

keyTerms.meaning: "How can you compare these?" A phrase used to reject a comparison.
Already bound by an oath, so a new oath cannot take effect

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives us the rule of מושבע ועומד: an oath cannot take effect on something already forbidden by an oath. The same idea drives the challenge at the end of this section.

phrases.english: Rava said: How can these be compared?!
There, he is liable for the general oath
phrases.notes: "There" means the oath about a deposit from Step 13.

phrases.english: and he is liable for the specific oath
since if he swears
and then swears again, he is liable for two.
Here, if it enters your mind
that the general oath takes effect
why would he be liable for the specific items?
He is already under oath!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 16 by showing that the deposit dispute does not apply to our oath.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the dispute about general and specific oaths in שבועת הפקדון applies to our oath not to eat.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It does not apply. With an oath not to eat, a general oath would leave the specific oaths with nothing to add, because he is already under oath. That is why the specific oaths are the ones that make him liable.

steps.title: The two halves of the משנה seem to contradict each other
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה and asks a question. Inedible food makes him exempt, yet non-kosher food (also unfit to eat) makes him liable. Why the difference?
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: "On my oath I will not eat," etc. The משנה itself is difficult! You said that if one swore "I will not eat" and then ate inedible foods or drank undrinkable liquids, he is exempt. Then it teaches that if he swore "I will not eat" and ate נבילות, טריפות, שקצים and רמשים, he is liable. Why is the first half exempt and the second half liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. It points out an apparent contradiction inside that משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both halves involve things people do not normally eat. Inedible food is unfit by nature, and non-kosher food is unfit because the תורה forbids it. So why does one make him exempt and the other make him liable?

keyTerms.meaning: "This itself is difficult." The source contradicts itself.
Meat of animals that died without proper שחיטה, and of animals with fatal defects
The first clause and the last clause of a teaching

phrases.english: "On my oath I will not eat," etc.
This itself is difficult:
You said: "On my oath I will not eat,"
and he ate foods that are not fit to eat

phrases.aramaic: וְשָׁתָה מַשְׁקִין שֶׁאֵין רְאוּיִן לִשְׁתִיָּה – פָּטוּר;
phrases.english: and drank liquids that are not fit to drink: he is exempt.
And then it teaches: "On my oath I will not eat,"
and he ate נבילות and טריפות,
repugnant creatures and creeping animals: he is liable.
What is different about the first clause, that he is exempt,
and what is different about the latter clause, that he is liable?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section on a different line of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rulings on inedible food and on non-kosher food
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both kinds of food are not normally eaten, so the rulings should match. Instead, one case is exempt and the other is liable.

steps.title: First half is an unspecified oath, second half names the items
steps.stepSummary: The first half is about a general oath not to eat, which does not cover inedible things. The second half is about a person who named the non-kosher items in his oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult. The first half is where he swore without saying what he meant. The second half is where he specifically named the items.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by showing that the two halves of the משנה describe different kinds of oaths.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plain "I will not eat" means normal food, so it does not include inedible things. When he names נבילות in his oath, the oath clearly covers them, so eating them makes him liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Unspecified, without explaining what is included
He specifies, naming exactly what the oath covers

phrases.english: This is not difficult:
the first clause is where he swore without specifying,
and the latter clause is where he specified.
phrases.notes: He named the non-kosher items in his oath, for example "I will not eat נבילות."

steps.triggerLanguage: הא לא קשיא רישא בסתם וסיפא במפרש
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each half describes a different kind of oath
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both halves are about the same general oath, so the rulings clash.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first half is a general oath, which leaves out inedible food. The second half is an oath that names the non-kosher items.

steps.title: But he is already sworn at הר סיני not to eat these
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer. Even if he named non-kosher food, how can his oath take effect? He is already under oath from הר סיני not to eat it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case where he specified should also be difficult on its own terms. Why is he liable? He is already under oath from הר סיני!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from Step 19. It says the case of a named oath has its own problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This uses the rule from Step 17: an oath cannot take effect on something already forbidden by an oath. The Jewish people accepted the תורה's prohibitions at הר סיני as if under oath. So a new personal oath against נבילות should have nothing left to forbid.

keyTerms.meaning: Already bound by oath from Sinai, since the תורה's prohibitions were accepted there like an oath
"Let it be difficult." Raises a problem.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא has gone back to the first contradiction. That one is resolved. This is a new problem with the answer itself: how can any personal oath take effect on food the תורה already forbids?

phrases.english: The case where he specified should also be difficult on its own:
Why is he liable? He is already under oath from Mount Sinai!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the second half of the משנה is about a person who named the items
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Non-kosher food is already forbidden by the oath taken at הר סיני. A new oath cannot take effect on something already sworn against, so naming the items should not make him liable.

steps.title: He included permitted foods together with the forbidden ones
steps.stepSummary: רב, שמואל and רבי יוחנן explain that the משנה's oath on non-kosher food works because he also included permitted foods in the same oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב, שמואל and רבי יוחנן say: the case is where he included permitted things together with the forbidden things in one oath.
steps.whatsHappening: Three great אמוראים answer the question from step 20. The oath covered permitted food and forbidden food together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An oath cannot normally take hold on something already forbidden by the oath of הר סיני. But here the oath clearly takes hold on the permitted foods. Since it is one oath that takes effect, it also reaches the forbidden foods. This is the idea of איסור כולל, a prohibition that includes more.

keyTerms.meaning: Includes; puts several items into one oath
Permitted things, such as kosher food
Forbidden things, such as נבילות and טריפות

phrases.english: Rav, Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan, who say:
It is where he includes permitted things
together with forbidden things.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20 about how an oath can take hold on food already forbidden from סיני.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the oath included permitted items too, so it takes hold as an איסור כולל.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An oath on non-kosher food alone cannot take effect, because of the oath from הר סיני.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because the oath includes permitted foods, it takes effect and covers the forbidden foods as well.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: it only works with a half-measure
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש answers differently. The oath only takes hold on a half-measure: either he spelled it out (according to the רבנן) or he made a plain oath (according to רבי עקיבא).
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: You can only find such a case in one of two ways. Either he specified a half-measure, according to the רבנן. Or he made a plain oath, according to רבי עקיבא, who says a person forbids himself on any amount at all.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש gives a second, different answer to the challenge of step 20. He says the oath can only take hold on less than the normal amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The oath from הר סיני brings liability for a full שיעור. A smaller amount leaves room for the personal oath to take hold. According to the רבנן, a plain oath means a full amount, so he must spell out 'half a שיעור'. According to רבי עקיבא, even a plain oath covers any amount, so no spelling out is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Specifies; says it explicitly in the oath
Half of the standard measure (less than a כזית)
With any amount at all, even a tiny bit

steps.confusionAlert: ריש לקיש is not giving two different answers of his own. He is showing how the משנה works under each side of a known dispute between the רבנן and רבי עקיבא.

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish said:
You cannot find it except
either where he specifies a half-measure,
phrases.notes: The liability from the oath at סיני is for a full amount, so a half-measure leaves room for his own oath.

phrases.english: and that is according to the Rabbis;
or with a plain oath,
according to Rabbi Akiva,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: אָדָם אוֹסֵר עַצְמוֹ בְּכׇל שֶׁהוּא.
phrases.english: who said: a person forbids himself with any amount.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר: אִי אַתָּה מוֹצֵא אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a competing answer to the same challenge that step 21 answered.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the oath takes hold on a half-measure, which the oath from סיני does not fully cover.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An oath on non-kosher food can never take effect because of the oath from סיני.
steps.terutzMaskana: It takes effect on a half-measure: spelled out according to the רבנן, or with a plain oath according to רבי עקיבא.

steps.title: Why does ריש לקיש not accept רבי יוחנן's answer?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא understands why רבי יוחנן rejects ריש לקיש's view, but asks why ריש לקיש rejects רבי יוחנן's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that רבי יוחנן did not say like ריש לקיש, because רבי יוחנן explains our משנה so that everyone agrees with it. But ריש לקיש, what is his reason for not saying like רבי יוחנן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא compares the two answers. It asks what ריש לקיש's problem is with רבי יוחנן's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's answer works for everyone. ריש לקיש's answer has to split the משנה between the רבנן and רבי עקיבא. A view that fits everyone is usually better, so why would ריש לקיש give it up?

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense that... (sets up a contrast with a question)
He establishes it; he explains the case this way

phrases.english: It makes sense that Rabbi Yochanan
did not say like Reish Lakish,
because he explains our Mishnah
according to everyone;
but Reish Lakish,

phrases.aramaic: מַאי טַעְמָא לָא אָמַר כְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן?
phrases.english: what is the reason he did not say like Rabbi Yochanan?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לָא אָמַר כְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two answers given in steps 21 and 22 and questions ריש לקיש's choice.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What flaw ריש לקיש sees in רבי יוחנן's answer of including permitted foods.

steps.title: ריש לקיש begins to explain his reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts ריש לקיש's answer: 'When we say an inclusive prohibition takes effect...' The sentence continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש would tell you: When we say that an איסור כולל takes effect...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins ריש לקיש's answer. It is setting up a limit on when an איסור כולל works, which will be finished in the next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's answer depends on the idea of איסור כולל. ריש לקיש is about to explain that this idea only works in certain cases. That would show why it cannot explain our משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: He would tell you (giving someone's likely reasoning)
An inclusive prohibition, which takes effect on more things and so can also take hold where there is already a prohibition

phrases.english: He would tell you:
When we say that an inclusive prohibition takes effect,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְךָ: כִּי אָמְרִינַן אִיסּוּר כּוֹלֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Opening of ריש לקיש's limit on איסור כולל. The answer is completed on the next amud.
